rationale: The author-posted journal copy, pp. 1779–1799, describes field-scale comparisons of management and farmland organisms in beet, maize and oilseed rape. The original design and results concern biodiversity and agricultural management. No dried-date exposure or clinical pain outcome is part of the study.

Chapter 2 of the first author's institutional thesis identifies the 2005 NeXT methods paper and reproduces its design. The examined recruitment section explicitly lists parkinsonism among exclusions. The study classifies nonmedical drug exposures and proposes imaging and cognitive or psychiatric assessments. It supplies no dried-date and Parkinson pain comparison.

The complete Iowa Women’s Health Study manuscript compares physical activity and quality of life in older women with and without cancer. The SF-36 includes bodily pain. The 127-item questionnaire supplied covariates and a composite diet score. The reported tables do not link dried dates to pain in Parkinson disease.

The published Mashhad occupational cohort protocol and baseline tables summarize diet as broad food-group intake and describe separate clinical and mood assessments. The original tables supply no item-specific dried-date and Parkinson pain comparison. The cohort design and initial measurements do not establish an intervention effect.

The original cardiac rehabilitation study compares exercise with education, exercise alone and usual care. It reports a diet-behavior score and addresses chest symptoms in cardiac education. The paper's outcomes concern cardiac rehabilitation and clinical follow-up. A food-specific Parkinson pain comparison falls outside the study design.

The published clinical case concerns supportive inpatient care for a person with a serious acute illness and coexisting Parkinson disease. Parkinson history is relevant to care context. The report does not measure dried-date intake, an isolated dietary intervention or a Parkinson pain comparison.

The author deposit preserves the journal article and figures for the bovine adrenal chromaffin graft study. The original comparison measures survival and tissue responses to different cell preparations in rats. Sagen is a byline surname. Dried-date intake and Parkinson pain are outside the experiment.

All five printed pages, 25–29, report neuropsychological testing in Parkinson and Alzheimer dementia groups with matched severity and a healthy comparison. The principal table compares memory and executive tasks. The article does not study culinary salmon or measure its effect on bradykinesia.

The original design and regression excerpts identify a 50-person mild-Parkinson cohort measured with dynamometry, motor scales and short- and longer-distance walking tests. Bradykinesia is a predictor in the walking models. Salmon is a byline surname. The study does not test a grilled-salmon effect.

The reproduced journal article, pp. 183–192, identifies Cohen-Salmon as a byline surname. The original group table and behavioral results compare a toxin model with controls across mouse genotypes. The anxiety test showed no detected toxin effect in the groups. This mouse comparison involved no poached salmon exposure.

All five printed pages, 7500–7504, report PET imaging during tone–airpuff eyeblink conditioning. Anxiety is discussed as one possible testing-state explanation. Salmon occurs as a cited surname. The experiment does not compare poached salmon or measure a change in Parkinson anxiety.

All three printed pages, 372–374, describe familial extrapyramidal signs and peripheral neuropathy. The biopsy section on page 373 uses onion bulbs for a nerve morphology that was absent in the specimen. It does not describe food intake. The familial motor findings provide neurological context without a raw-onion rigidity comparison.
